RagShortTexts: Valentinian's western government remains within the Roman imperial system in 374.
Military supply, taxation, office and patronage shape western elite competition.

Variants.Content: In 374 Valentinian's western government remains part of the Roman imperial system. Military commands, court offices, senatorial wealth and provincial administration offer distinct sources of influence, not a single feudal ladder. Frontier operations require taxes, transport and recruits, while powerful landowners and officials dispute how burdens fall. Patronage can secure a hearing or protect a client, but judicial investigations can also expose an entire network. The western faction in the module is a division of imperial rule, not an already permanent separate nation. Its conflicts should concern actual offices, resources and access to authority rather than assume every senator keeps a private hereditary army.

A western soldier experiences an imperial policy as a march, a ration issue or another period on the frontier. If civil and military officials quarrel over transport, he still needs grain before moving. Changing the name of a commander does not repair a shield; men remember which promises reached the camp and which remained on a clerk's tablet.

A wealthy notable can use estates and connections to seek influence, but must deal with officials whose demands need not match his own. An imperial audience may help one petition while creating obligations to a patron. Protecting a household's position requires navigating service and taxation, not merely hiding steel behind a banquet smile.
